title: Sort a K-Sorted Array
statement:
An array of `n` integers is **k-sorted** (also called nearly sorted) if every element is at most `k` positions away from the index it would occupy in the fully sorted array. When there are equal values, it is enough that some sorted arrangement exists in which every element is within `k` positions of its current index.

You are given a k-sorted array and the value `k`. Print the array in non-decreasing order.

Plain sorting costs `O(n log n)`. The interviewer wants you to exploit `k` and do better when `k` is small.

**Follow-up:** aim for `O(n log k)` time using a min-heap.
inputFormat:
The first line contains two integers `n` and `k`.
The second line contains `n` space-separated integers. The array is guaranteed to be k-sorted.
outputFormat: Print the `n` integers in non-decreasing order, separated by spaces.

examples.explanation: Every element is at most 2 positions from its sorted place (for example, 3 is at index 0 and belongs at index 2). The sorted array is 1 2 3 4 5 6 7.
Adjacent pairs are swapped, so each element is exactly one step from its target.

hints: The smallest element of the whole array must be among the first k + 1 positions.
Keep a min-heap of a sliding group of k + 1 elements: pop the minimum to the output, then push the next element from the input.
When the input is exhausted, keep popping the heap until it is empty.
